claims.text: Aging HfNbTaTiZr at 600–800 °C induces nanoscale precipitate formation.
The precipitates are Ta/Zr-rich clusters located both at grain boundaries and within grains.
The nanoscale precipitates locally alter the elastic modulus of the alloy.
The nanoscale precipitates have a different coefficient of thermal expansion from the surrounding matrix.
Thermal-expansion mismatch between precipitates and matrix generates internal thermal stresses during heating up to 1250 °C.
The mismatch-induced thermal stresses impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion increases the yield strength of aged HfNbTaTiZr.
Precipitate-induced dislocation pinning improves creep resistance at 1250 °C.
Aged samples exhibit greater hardening during cold rolling than homogenized samples.
Aged samples exhibit anomalous thermal-expansion behavior indicative of internal thermal stresses.
Precipitation produces measurable deviations in elastic modulus and thermal expansion.
The proposed precipitate-mismatch mechanism provides a unified explanation for creep behavior, cold-rolling hardening, and thermoelastic response.
The homogenized solution-treated baseline has a uniform microstructure without pronounced nanoscale precipitates.
The homogenized baseline exhibits more uniform stress–strain and thermal-expansion behavior than the aged state.
Changes in interstitial content and partitioning can alter lattice distortion and hardness, potentially mimicking effects attributed to precipitates.
Dislocation slip and dislocation density are relevant to deformation in a closely related NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy.
Comparing otherwise identically processed solution-treated and aged samples is intended to isolate the effect of aging-associated precipitates.

A lack of significant aged-versus-baseline differences, or the absence of the proposed precipitates with only interstitial partitioning observed, would reject precipitates as the dominant unified cause.
